riskToHumans.metaTitle: Risk to humans — what harmless, moderate, and high mean
riskToHumans.metaDescription: Georgia’s reptiles are labelled harmless, moderate, or high risk to people. What each level means, which species it covers, and what to do if you meet one.
riskToHumans.keywords: risk to humans, snake risk Georgia, venomous snakes Georgia, high risk viper, moderate risk, harmless snakes, Macrovipera lebetina, risk levels reptiles
riskToHumans.title: Risk to humans
riskToHumans.subtitle: This atlas uses three labels: harmless, moderate, and high. Here is what each one means — and what to do if you meet the animal.
riskToHumans.scaleTitle: A field label, not a medical diagnosis
riskToHumans.scaleLead: The badge on a species page is this atlas’s classification of medical risk to people in Georgia. It is not a lab ranking of venom potency, not a measure of how “aggressive” the animal is, and not the same as conservation status.
riskToHumans.scaleDisclaimer: Educational page — not emergency medical advice. If bitten, call 112.
riskToHumans.scaleHighBody: A bite can cause severe local and systemic illness. Keep distance. If bitten, this is an emergency.
riskToHumans.scaleModerateBody: Venomous, with a lower typical profile than the highest-risk vipers — a bite still needs medical care.
riskToHumans.scaleHarmlessBody: Most species here. No medically significant venom. Do not pick them up anyway — handling stresses the animal and can confuse lookalikes.
riskToHumans.HighLead: In this atlas, high risk means a medically serious bite: local tissue damage and possible systemic effects that need hospital care. These are not animals that hunt people. Most bites happen when someone tries to catch, kill, or move the snake.
riskToHumans.HighPoint1Body: Two vipers: the Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetina) — Georgia’s largest venomous snake, with the highest typical venom yield — and the Transcaucasian long-nosed viper (Vipera transcaucasiana). Both can cause a life-threatening bite.
riskToHumans.HighPoint2Body: Do not handle it. Step back or go around. Even for a photo, do not close in. The snake will usually leave if it has a way out.
riskToHumans.HighPoint3Body: Call 112 immediately. Stay as still as you can and do not move the bitten limb. Do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet. This page does not replace a clinician.
riskToHumans.HighSpeciesBody: Open a profile for identification, range, and encounter notes.
riskToHumans.ModerateLead: Venomous, and a bite is a medical event — but the typical outcome is assessed below the two high-risk vipers. “Moderate” is not “mild”: it still means keep distance and get care after a bite.
riskToHumans.ModeratePoint1Body: Four Vipera — Caucasus, Dinnik’s, Darevsky’s, and steppe — plus one rear-fanged species, the eastern Montpellier snake (Malpolon insignitus). The rear-fanged bite is usually milder; it should still be taken seriously.
riskToHumans.ModeratePoint2Body: The same rule as for high risk: do not pick it up, do not corner it, do not try to move it. Distance settles most encounters.
riskToHumans.ModeratePoint3Body: Call 112. A moderate-risk bite can still cause painful swelling and needs a medical assessment. Do not wait to “see if it gets worse.”
riskToHumans.ModerateSpeciesBody: Vipers first, then the rear-fanged species. Each profile states why the risk sits here and not higher.
riskToHumans.HarmlessLead: No medically significant venom. This is the default for lizards, turtles, amphibians, and most snakes in Georgia. Harmless does not mean “pick it up” — and it does not mean the animal never bites if handled.
riskToHumans.HarmlessPoint1Body: A bite from these species is not a venom emergency. Several harmless snakes flatten the head or hiss so they look like a viper. Identification belongs on the species page, not in the hand.
riskToHumans.HarmlessPoint2Body: Watch it and leave it where it is. Handling stresses the animal, can spread disease in amphibians, and leaves a risk of confusing a viper for a lookalike.
riskToHumans.HarmlessPoint3Body: Wash your hands. Amphibian skin produces mucus or defensive secretions; moving animals between ponds spreads fungal disease. A hard bite from a large harmless snake is still a wound — clean it, and seek care if it needs stitches.
riskToHumans.HarmlessSpeciesBody: Grass snakes, the smooth snake, the cat snake, and the glass lizard are the mix-ups this atlas sees most. The rest of the harmless catalog is in the atlas filter.

riskToHumans.faqIntro: Short answers on the three-level scale. Full species detail lives on each profile.
riskToHumans.faq1Q: What does the badge on a species page mean?
riskToHumans.faq1A: It is this atlas’s label for medical risk to people: harmless, moderate, or high. Clicking it opens this page, scrolled to that level. It is not IUCN status and not a score for how likely the animal is to approach you.
riskToHumans.faq2Q: Does “harmless” mean it will not bite?
riskToHumans.faq2A: No. Harmless means no medically significant venom. A large colubrid can still bite hard if handled. Several harmless snakes mimic vipers when threatened. Leave the animal where it is.
riskToHumans.faq3Q: Why is the Montpellier snake moderate if it is not a viper?
riskToHumans.faq3A: Malpolon insignitus is rear-fanged, not a viper. Risk to people is usually milder than a viper bite, but it is still medically relevant in this atlas — treat a bite seriously and call 112.
riskToHumans.faq4Q: Which snakes are high risk in Georgia?
riskToHumans.faq4A: Two: the Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetina) and the Transcaucasian long-nosed viper (Vipera transcaucasiana). Other vipers in the atlas are moderate. A bite from any of them needs medical care.
riskToHumans.faq5Q: Are lizards, turtles, or amphibians ever high risk?
riskToHumans.faq5A: Not in this atlas. Venom risk to people applies to certain snakes. Lizards, turtles, and amphibians are labelled harmless. Do not pick them up; wash hands after any contact.

seo.title: How the regional atlas works
seo.p1: In Georgia, reptile assemblages shift with place: Colchic forests and the western coast, the Greater Caucasus high belt, and the arid basins of the east each support different species. The regional atlas turns that gradient into a practical path — pick a place on the map or in the list and see what is recorded there.
seo.p2: Each region page brings together confirmed species lists, habitats, venomous-snake notes, and a map. Amphibians, turtles, and almost all lizards (except the glass lizard) are not mapped yet — that is a gap, not a complete fauna. The full snake regional view is also on the range guide.

seo.reptilesP1: Georgia sits between the Black Sea, the Greater Caucasus, and the arid east — a short geographic span that supports vipers of high mountains and Colchic forests, water snakes of rivers and wetlands, racers of dry foothills, and a widespread legless lizard often mistaken for a snake. Reptile profiles here are bilingual, with Georgia-specific range notes and field photography.
seo.reptilesP2: Species richness here is shaped by elevation, humidity, and refuge habitats. Western Colchic landscapes favor moisture-linked snakes such as Natrix; eastern semi-arid basins hold Macrovipera lebetina and fast colubrids; alpine and subalpine belts hold Caucasus endemics including Vipera dinniki. This section is about reptiles — snakes, lizards, and turtles.
seo.amphibiansP1: Frogs, toads, newts, and the Caucasian salamander sit in the same catalog, with dedicated guides. This is not a complete national list — only published profiles.
seo.birdsP1: Bird profiles follow the same rule: named sources, no invented maps. The list is growing and does not replace the national avifauna checklist.
seo.mammalsP1: Mammal pages use the same profile structure. Few are published yet — absence from this catalog does not mean the species is absent from Georgia.
seo.spidersP1: Spider pages follow the same rule: named sources, no invented maps. The list is growing and does not replace a full arachnofauna checklist.
seo.venomousP1: Only a minority of Georgia’s snakes are medically significant. In this atlas, “venomous” means moderate or high risk to humans: the Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetina), Caucasus viper (Vipera kaznakovi), Dinnik’s viper (Vipera dinniki), Transcaucasian long-nosed viper (Vipera transcaucasiana), Darevsky’s viper (Vipera darevskii), and steppe viper (Vipera renardi). Most other snakes here — grass snake, dice snake, racers, smooth snake, cat snake — are harmless to people, though several are frequently misidentified.
seo.venomousP2: Safe encounter practice is simple: do not handle wild snakes, keep distance, and learn the lookalikes common in your region. Open each profile for identification traits, habitat, and conservation status. This is educational natural-history guidance, not emergency medical advice.
seo.venomousGuideCta: Full guide: venomous snakes in Georgia
seo.regionsP1: Distribution in the atlas is recorded by Georgia’s administrative regions as a practical field layer — from Abkhazia and Adjara on the humid west to Kakheti and Kvemo Kartli in the dry east, plus the capital district of Tbilisi. A species may appear in several regions; endemics and elevational specialists are more narrowly placed.
seo.regionsP2: Use the map to move from place to fauna, then open regional pages for habitats, safety notes, and the local species list. For research-grade occurrence data, profiles also cite databases such as GBIF and the Reptile Database alongside IUCN assessments where available.

venomousSnakes.safetyStep1Body: Never catch or move a wild snake — most bites happen during handling.
venomousSnakes.safetyStep2Body: Pass aside or back away. Even for a photo, do not close in.
venomousSnakes.safetyStep3Body: Many harmless snakes resemble vipers. Killing by mistake harms the ecosystem.
venomousSnakes.safetyStep4Body: Call 112 immediately. Stay calm and do not move the bitten arm or leg. Do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet. This does not replace a doctor’s advice.

venomousSnakes.faq1Q: How many venomous snakes are there in Georgia?
venomousSnakes.faq1A: This atlas treats six vipers as medically significant: the Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetinus), Transcaucasian long-nosed viper, Caucasus viper, Dinnik’s viper, Darevsky’s viper, and steppe viper. In addition, the eastern Montpellier snake (Malpolon insignitus) is a moderate-risk rear-fanged species — not a viper.
venomousSnakes.faq2Q: Which venomous snake is the most dangerous?
venomousSnakes.faq2A: The Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetina) is Georgia’s largest and most dangerous venomous snake; its bite can threaten human life. The Transcaucasian long-nosed viper is also high risk; the Caucasus, Dinnik’s, Darevsky’s, and steppe vipers are assessed as moderate risk.
venomousSnakes.faq3Q: Where do venomous snakes occur in Georgia?
venomousSnakes.faq3A: The Levantine viper favors dry rocky east; the Caucasus viper Colchic forests and the western coast; Dinnik’s viper the high Greater Caucasus; the Transcaucasian long-nosed viper the Meskheti–Trialeti ranges; Darevsky’s viper the Javakheti–Erusheti highlands; the steppe viper Javakheti plateaus and eastern steppes. Exact regions are on each species profile and in the regional atlas.
venomousSnakes.faq4Q: How do I tell a venomous snake from a harmless one?
venomousSnakes.faq4A: Vipers often have a vertical pupil and a more triangular head; many harmless snakes have a round pupil. The rule is not foolproof — learn species traits and habitat from the profiles instead.
venomousSnakes.faq5Q: What should I do if bitten?
venomousSnakes.faq5A: Seek medical care immediately. Stay calm, do not move the bitten arm or leg, and avoid home remedies (cutting, sucking, tourniquets). This page is educational and does not replace a clinician.

turtles.faq1Q: How many turtle species are there in Georgia?
turtles.faq1A: This atlas lists four species: spur-thighed tortoise, European pond turtle, Caspian turtle, and the introduced red-eared slider — following Tarkhnishvili et al. 2026.
turtles.faq2Q: Which turtles are native in Georgia?
turtles.faq2A: Three are native: spur-thighed tortoise (Testudo graeca), European pond turtle (Emys orbicularis), and Caspian turtle (Mauremys caspica). The red-eared slider is introduced.
turtles.faq3Q: Which turtles are land turtles and which are water turtles?
turtles.faq3A: Only the spur-thighed tortoise is terrestrial. Pond, Caspian, and red-eared slider turtles are freshwater species.
turtles.faq4Q: How do I tell turtle species apart?
turtles.faq4A: Start with land vs water, then shell and head marks. Full comparison is on the <identify>turtle identification</identify> guide; concrete traits are on each species profile.
turtles.faq5Q: Where do turtles occur in Georgia?
turtles.faq5A: The land tortoise uses open dry habitats; water turtles use ponds and wetlands. Verified regions are on each profile and in the regional atlas — the map only colours named records.
turtles.faq6Q: How do I recognise a red-eared slider?
turtles.faq6A: T. s. elegans often has a broad red stripe behind the eye; native water turtles lack that mark. Status is introduced — details are on the profile.
turtles.faq7Q: What is the difference between the pond turtle and the Caspian turtle?
turtles.faq7A: Both are native freshwater turtles from different families. The pond turtle is Emydidae; the Caspian turtle is Geoemydidae. Field marks and range are on the profiles — we do not repeat a full comparison here.
turtles.faq8Q: Can I take a turtle home?
turtles.faq8A: Do not take wild turtles home — collection harms populations. Observe, photograph, and compare with the atlas. This page is a field atlas and does not give keeping or legal advice.

snakeIdentify.metaTitle: How to tell venomous from harmless snakes in Georgia
snakeIdentify.metaDescription: Venomous vs harmless snakes in Georgia: visual cues are not universal. Giurza, Caucasian viper, water snakes, and the glass lizard — compare profiles.

snakeIdentify.heroImageAlt: Venomous viper in forest and harmless grass snake by a stream — comparison
snakeIdentify.title: Venomous or harmless?
snakeIdentify.subtitle: Most snakes in Georgia are harmless. A vertical pupil and a triangular head often point to vipers, but no rule is universal.
snakeIdentify.guideP1: Telling venomous from harmless by a photo is risky. A species profile is better: marks, habitat, region. This page gathers common mix-ups — not a field guarantee.
snakeIdentify.guideP2: Start with the Levantine viper and the <kaznakovi>Caucasus viper (Vipera kaznakovi)</kaznakovi>, then the other venomous species. Water snakes, the smooth snake, and the glass lizard (a lizard) are often mistaken for vipers.
snakeIdentify.signsTitle: What people look at — and why it is not enough
snakeIdentify.signsWarning: No single sign proves a snake is venomous. If you are unsure, keep your distance and compare with the atlas.
snakeIdentify.sign1Body: Vipers often have a vertical pupil; many harmless snakes have a round one. It is not always visible and it changes with light.
snakeIdentify.sign2Body: A triangular head is typical of vipers, but a harmless snake can flatten its head when threatened.
snakeIdentify.sign3Body: The grass snake can resemble the Caucasian viper; the glass lizard resembles a snake. Compare the pairs below and open the profiles.
snakeIdentify.sign4Body: Do not catch it. Do not kill it. Most are harmless. The venomous list is in a separate guide.

snakeIdentify.chainBody: Start with the most dangerous, then the western forest viper, then the rest of the catalog.
snakeIdentify.pairsBody: Water snake and viper; glass lizard and snake; Montpellier snake and giurza. Each side opens a profile.
snakeIdentify.faqIntro: Short answers — the decision lives on the profile.
snakeIdentify.faq1Q: How do I tell a venomous snake from a harmless one?
snakeIdentify.faq1A: The reliable path is species identification, not a single cue. Pupil and head shape often help, but they are not universal.
snakeIdentify.faq2Q: Is the glass lizard a venomous snake?
snakeIdentify.faq2A: No. It is a legless lizard: it has eyelids and an ear opening. The profile shows how it differs from water snakes.
snakeIdentify.faq3Q: Which venomous snake should I learn first?
snakeIdentify.faq3A: Giurza (largest and most dangerous) and the Caucasian viper (west, often confused with the grass snake). Then the rest of the venomous guide.
snakeIdentify.faq4Q: Can I identify a snake from a photo with certainty?
snakeIdentify.faq4A: Often not. Use the atlas to compare, and if there is a bite — call 112. Do not wait on identification.

snakeBite.metaDescription: Snakebite in Georgia: call 112 immediately. What to do, what not to do, and possible symptoms. Do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet. Educational page — not a medical protocol.
snakeBite.keywords: snakebite Georgia, snake bite what to do, 112, venomous snake bite, snakebite symptoms
snakeBite.heroImageAlt: Levantine viper on a rocky slope — cover for Georgia’s venomous-snake guide
snakeBite.title: Snakebite in Georgia — what should you do?
snakeBite.subtitle: If a snake has bitten you, the first step is 112. This page is educational and does not replace a clinician or emergency care.
snakeBite.disclaimerTitle: Bitten by a snake? Call 112 immediately
snakeBite.disclaimerBody: If a snake has bitten you in Georgia, call 112 immediately and seek emergency medical care. Keep movement to a minimum. Do not cut the wound, suck venom, apply a tourniquet, or attempt to capture the snake.
snakeBite.summary2: Move away from the snake and limit movement.
snakeBite.summary3: Do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet.
snakeBite.summary4: Do not catch the snake or delay care to identify the species.
snakeBite.disclaimerNote: Only medical staff decide treatment. The steps here are educational first-response points based on WHO, CDC, and 112 public guidance — not an antivenom protocol.
snakeBite.doTitle: What to do after a snakebite
snakeBite.do1Body: Immediately. 112 is Georgia’s single emergency number — police, fire, and ambulance. Do not wait for symptoms.
snakeBite.do2Body: Get to a safe place. Do not approach the animal again, and do not try to catch or kill it.
snakeBite.do3Body: Sit or lie down somewhere safe and limit unnecessary movement until help arrives.
snakeBite.do4Title: Keep the bitten limb as still as you can
snakeBite.do4Body: Keep the bitten arm or leg as still as possible. This is educational guidance — not a full clinical protocol.
snakeBite.do5Body: Rings, watches, bracelets, or tight clothing near the bite can cause harm if swelling develops.
snakeBite.do6Body: Home remedies do not replace medical care. If possible, do not drive yourself — symptoms can affect you.
snakeBite.dont1Body: Cutting or excising the wound does not remove venom and causes harm.
snakeBite.dont2Body: Sucking venom by mouth or device does not work and damages the wound.
snakeBite.dont3Body: A tight arterial tourniquet is not recommended for snakebite and can cause serious harm.
snakeBite.dont4Title: Do not catch or handle the snake
snakeBite.dont4Body: Catching a snake — even a dead one — often causes another bite. Identification from a distance or a photo is enough, and only if safe.
snakeBite.dont5Title: Do not use alcohol or folk remedies
snakeBite.dont5Body: Alcohol, ice, electric shock, or other unproven methods are not treatment and waste time.
snakeBite.dont6Title: Do not delay care to identify the species
snakeBite.dont6Body: Call 112 and seek care first. Species ID must not delay the emergency call.
snakeBite.symptomsIntro: Symptoms vary with species, venom, bite location, amount of venom, and other factors. The list below is possible signs — not a diagnostic checklist.
snakeBite.symptomsUrgent: Do not wait for symptoms before calling 112. Absence of symptoms does not mean the bite is safe.
snakeBite.symptomsNote: Local and general signs mainly follow the CDC public list; serious effects of envenoming follow the WHO fact sheet. The list is not complete. For severe or unusual symptoms, call 112.
snakeBite.dangerTitle: When is a snakebite especially dangerous?
snakeBite.dangerIntro: Every suspected bite is an emergency for 112. Below are situations that need especially fast response.
snakeBite.danger1: Difficulty breathing, severe swelling, or systemic symptoms.
snakeBite.danger2: Children often experience more severe effects because of smaller body mass.
snakeBite.danger3: Delaying care increases risk — do not postpone transport to a health facility.
snakeBite.danger4: If you did not see the snake but suspect a bite — still seek emergency care.
snakeBite.venomBody: No. Many snakes in Georgia are not venomous to people, though a bite can still cause injury or infection. The atlas lists <venomous>venomous species</venomous> whose bites are medically important. Species comparison belongs in the <identify>identification guide</identify>, not at the bite scene.
snakeBite.venomNote: Do not try to judge medical risk yourself. That decision belongs to medical staff.
snakeBite.unseenEyebrow: If you did not see the snake
snakeBite.unseenTitle: What if I did not see the snake?
snakeBite.unseenBody: Still call 112 and seek emergency care. Do not delay the call to identify the species. If you can observe safely from a distance or take a photo, that may help later — never approach or catch the animal.
snakeBite.unseenId: Species comparison later — in the <identify>venomous snake ID guide</identify>, only after emergency care is underway.
snakeBite.sourcesTitle: What this page is based on
snakeBite.sourcesIntro: Medical recommendations cite external authoritative sources. Species and range information come from the Reptiles.ge atlas. This page is not an independent medical authority.
snakeBite.sourceExt1Body: Georgia’s single emergency number. After a bite, this is the first action.
snakeBite.sourceExt2Body: Move away from the bite area, remove tight items, immobilize; avoid tight arterial tourniquets, wound incision/excision, venom suction, and traditional methods; transport promptly to a health facility.
snakeBite.sourceExt3Body: Possible effects of envenoming: paralysis, bleeding disorders, tissue damage; children may experience more severe effects.
snakeBite.sourceExt4Title: CDC / NIOSH — Venomous snakes first aid
snakeBite.sourceExt4Body: Emergency care without waiting for symptoms; remove rings/watches; do not cut, suck, or tourniquet; do not catch the snake; do not drink alcohol.
snakeBite.sourceSite1Title: Venomous snakes guide and species profiles
snakeBite.sourceSite1Body: Georgia’s venomous species list, risk levels, and identification — from atlas data, not a medical protocol.
snakeBite.sourceSite2Body: Page structure and wording are prepared by Reptiles.ge from the sources above. The site is not a medical institution.
snakeBite.editorialBody: This page is prepared by Reptiles.ge. Medical recommendations are checked against the cited official and medical sources. Species information follows the site atlas.
snakeBite.editorialDisclaimer: The page is educational and does not replace a clinician, toxicologist, or emergency service.

snakeBite.speciesBody: Below are the atlas’s {count} venomous species — for identification, not for decisions at the bite scene. Full context: <venomous>venomous guide</venomous>, <index>species index</index>, <range>range</range>. After a bite, call 112 first.
snakeBite.faqIntro: Short answers for an urgent situation. Detail is above; medical decisions belong with 112 and clinicians.
snakeBite.ctaBody: Species comparison and prevention live on profiles and guides. After a bite, 112 still comes first.
snakeBite.faq1Q: What should I do first after a snakebite?
snakeBite.faq1A: Call 112 immediately — do not wait for symptoms. Move away from the snake, limit movement, and keep the bitten limb still. Do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet.
snakeBite.faq2A: No. WHO and CDC rule out cutting the wound — it causes harm.
snakeBite.faq3Q: Can I suck out the venom?
snakeBite.faq3A: No. Sucking venom does not work and damages the wound.
snakeBite.faq4A: No. A tight arterial tourniquet is not recommended for snakebite.
snakeBite.faq5A: No. Many snakes are non-venomous, though a bite can still injure. Do not judge risk yourself — call 112.
snakeBite.faq6Q: What symptoms can a snakebite cause?
snakeBite.faq6A: Pain, swelling, bleeding, weakness, nausea, breathing difficulty, or neurological signs may occur. Absence of symptoms does not mean safety.
snakeBite.faq7Q: Should I catch the snake so doctors know the species?
snakeBite.faq7A: No. Catching it often causes another bite. A distant look or photo is enough if safe.
snakeBite.faq8Q: What if I did not see the snake?
snakeBite.faq8A: Still call 112. Do not delay the call for identification. Species comparison can wait.

lizardIdentify.subtitle: Telling Georgia’s lizards apart starts with a photo and size, but for Darevskia colour is not enough — you need region and a profile.
lizardIdentify.guideTitle: From a photo to a profile — not colour alone
lizardIdentify.guideP1: Rock lizards (Darevskia) are numerous in the Caucasus and look alike. The Caucasian agama is an agamid; the glass lizard is a legless lizard, not a snake.
lizardIdentify.guideP2: Below is a field order: photo → size → colour → range → lookalikes. The decision lives on the profile, not as a guarantee on this page.
lizardIdentify.flowBody: Each step narrows the choice. If you are unsure, open profiles and compare.
lizardIdentify.step1Body: Look at head shape, scales, limbs. A legless body may be a glass lizard or a slow worm — not necessarily a snake.
lizardIdentify.step2Body: The glass lizard is about 1–1.35 m on its profile; the slow worm is smaller there — no length figure is given. Darevskia and the agama are smaller rock lizards. Numbers come from profile stats only.
lizardIdentify.step3Body: Colour is not enough for Darevskia — one species varies. Use other marks and region.
lizardIdentify.step4Body: If you know the place, open the region page. Maps for many lizards are still empty — that is a gap, not “does not occur”.
lizardIdentify.step5Body: Compare the pairs below and open the profiles. Glass lizard vs snake has its own comparison guide.
lizardIdentify.darevskiaBody: Caucasian rock lizards sit close together in appearance. Profile and region beat guessing by colour. The list below opens profiles.

lizardIdentify.faq3Q: Is a legless lizard a snake?

lizardCompare.metaTitle: Lizard or glass lizard — how it differs from a snake
lizardCompare.metaDescription: Glass lizard vs slow worm vs snake in Georgia. Eyelids, ear opening, side fold, size — from profiles only. None of the three is venomous.

lizardCompare.heroImageAlt: European glass lizard in dry grassland
lizardCompare.title: Lizard, glass lizard, or snake?
lizardCompare.subtitle: The glass lizard is a legless lizard. The slow worm is a smaller legless lizard. Water snakes are snakes. None of these three is venomous.
lizardCompare.guideP1: The glass lizard profile states movable eyelids, external ear openings, and a side fold — snakes do not have eyelids. Length is about 1–1.35 m; it is harmless.
lizardCompare.guideP2: The slow worm (Anguis colchica) is a candidate species in the checklist; on its profile it is smaller than the glass lizard and smoother — no length figure is given. Water snakes are snakes. Marks and sizes come only from these profiles.
lizardCompare.tableBody: An em dash means this page’s sources do not state that mark for that species — not that it lacks the trait.
lizardCompare.alsoTitle: The dice snake is a snake too
lizardCompare.alsoBody: Natrix tessellata is the same genus as the grass snake — a snake, not a lizard. It often appears with the glass lizard in lookalike lists.
lizardCompare.faqTitle: What people ask about this comparison
lizardCompare.faqIntro: Only marks confirmed on the profiles.
lizardCompare.faq1Q: Is the glass lizard a snake or a lizard?
lizardCompare.faq1A: A lizard. Unlike a snake it has movable eyelids, external ear openings, and a side fold.
lizardCompare.faq2Q: How does it differ from the slow worm?
lizardCompare.faq2A: On its profile the slow worm is smaller and smoother; no length figure is given. The glass lizard is about 1–1.35 m and has a clear side fold. Both are harmless. The slow worm is a checklist candidate.
lizardCompare.faq3A: No. The profile classifies it as harmless.
lizardCompare.faq4A: Grass snakes and dice snakes are snakes often mixed up with legless lizards. They are harmless, but they are snakes.

turtleIdentify.flowTitle: How to identify a turtle in Georgia
turtleIdentify.flowBody: Start with where you saw it. Then, for water turtles, check for a red ear stripe. If that mark is absent, compare the pond turtle and the Caspian turtle.
turtleIdentify.step1Title: Step 1 — where did you see it?
turtleIdentify.step1Body: Walking on open, dry ground with a high dome — land branch. Pond, lake, marsh, or basking on a bank — water branch.
turtleIdentify.branchLandBody: High domed shell, columnar unwebbed legs, slow walking on dry or open ground.
turtleIdentify.branchLandAlt: Spur-thighed tortoise with a high domed shell on land
turtleIdentify.branchWaterBody: Flatter shell, webbed feet; pond, lake, marsh, or basking on the bank.
turtleIdentify.branchWaterAlt: Freshwater turtle with a flatter shell by water
turtleIdentify.landResultBody: Georgia’s only land tortoise. Separated from water turtles by the dome, columnar legs, and often thigh spurs.
turtleIdentify.step2Title: Step 2 — water turtle: red mark behind the eye?
turtleIdentify.step2Body: T. s. elegans has a broad red or orange stripe behind the eye. If that mark is clear — introduced slider. If not — compare the two native freshwater turtles.
turtleIdentify.branchSliderBody: Broad red stripe behind the eye, flatter shell; often in city ponds near Tbilisi and Batumi.
turtleIdentify.branchSliderAlt: Red-eared slider — broad red stripe behind the eye
turtleIdentify.branchNativeBody: Native freshwater turtles: European pond turtle (Emys) or Caspian turtle (Mauremys). Side-by-side comparison below.
turtleIdentify.branchNativeAlt: Native water turtle without a red ear stripe
turtleIdentify.sliderResultBody: An introduced species; wild populations are confirmed near Tbilisi and Batumi. Not native.
turtleIdentify.emysVsTitle: Pond turtle or Caspian turtle — how to tell them apart
turtleIdentify.emysVsBody: Both are native freshwater turtles and lack the slider’s red ear stripe. Below are the most useful field marks for telling them apart.
turtleIdentify.emysVsEmysCaption: Often a dark shell with yellow dots; head and neck dark with dots or short streaks.
turtleIdentify.emysVsMauremysCaption: Pale lengthwise neck stripes often present; shell usually more striped than speckled.

emys.shell: Low, oval; usually dark olive, brown, or black; often yellow dots or streaks.
emys.headNeck: Dark head, neck, and legs with yellow dots or short streaks; no red ear stripe.
emys.plastron: Paler plastron; Emys has a movable hinge.
emys.habitat: Freshwater ponds, lakes, and marshes; webbed feet; often basks on banks.
emys.range: Western and eastern Georgia (per profile); the map does not yet fully shade eastern regions.

mauremys.shell: Flatter than a land-tortoise dome; usually more striped than speckled.
mauremys.headNeck: Pale lengthwise neck stripes often present; no red ear stripe.
mauremys.plastron: Practically rigid — lacks the Emys hinge.
mauremys.habitat: Ponds, lakes, and slow waters; webbed feet; often basks on banks.
mauremys.range: Southeastern Georgia (Tarkhnishvili et al. 2026); figure specimen from Lisi Lake (Tbilisi) is a locality, not a full map.

turtleIdentify.faqIntro: Answers that do not merely repeat the key.
turtleIdentify.faq1Q: What is the difference between the pond turtle and the Caspian turtle?
turtleIdentify.faq1A: Emys often has a dark shell with yellow dots and a movable plastron hinge; Mauremys often has pale lengthwise neck stripes and a practically rigid plastron. Neither has a red ear stripe.
turtleIdentify.faq2Q: Can I take a turtle home?
turtleIdentify.faq2A: Do not take wild turtles. The spur-thighed tortoise is on Georgia’s Red List (VU) and in CITES Appendix II. The slider is a pet species, but releasing it into the wild creates new introduced populations.
turtleIdentify.faq3A: No. It is introduced; wild populations are confirmed near Tbilisi and Batumi.
turtleIdentify.faq4Q: Can I release a pet turtle into the wild?
turtleIdentify.faq4A: No. The checklist treats the slider as a pet and an unintentional introduction. Do not release pet turtles into ponds or lakes.

snakesInYard.metaTitle: How to get snakes out of the yard — what works and what doesn’t
snakesInYard.metaDescription: Snakes in the yard: there is no 100% snake repellent. Reduce shelter and food so snakes do not stay. What works in Georgia — and which myths waste your time.
snakesInYard.keywords: how to get rid of snakes in the yard, snakes in yard, snake repellent, snake in garden, sulfur snake myth, milk for snakes, Georgia snakes yard
snakesInYard.heroImageAlt: A specialist safely capturing a snake in a residential yard with professional tongs
snakesInYard.title: How to get snakes out of the yard
snakesInYard.subtitle: There is no reliable way to “drive them out” on command. Make the yard poor for shelter and food — then a snake will not stay.
snakesInYard.whyTitle: Why do snakes enter a yard?
snakesInYard.whyLead: No method repels snakes with 100% effect. A yard usually attracts them for two reasons — shelter and food.
snakesInYard.whyShelterBody: Tall grass, shrubs, logs, stones, building materials, and wall cracks make good cover.
snakesInYard.whyFoodBody: Rodents are prey for many snakes. If mice or rats thrive in the yard, conditions improve for snakes too.
snakesInYard.coverImageAlt: A snake on rocks near rodents and tall grass — shelter and food in one place
snakesInYard.coverCaption: A yard attracts snakes when it offers shelter (rocks, logs, tall grass) and food (rodents).
snakesInYard.actionsTitle: What to do so they stop coming in
snakesInYard.actionsLead: The goal is not to kill or catch a snake — it is to manage the yard so neither shelter nor food remains.
snakesInYard.action1Title: Regular clearing of grass in the yard
snakesInYard.action1Body: Cut tall grass — the area becomes more open and less attractive to snakes.
snakesInYard.action2Body: Fill burrows and holes, reduce dense shrubs along edges, seal cracks in walls, and clear logs, stones, and building materials from the yard — snakes often hide there.
snakesInYard.action3Body: Rodents are food for snakes. If mice or rats are present, address that first — conditions for snakes worsen on their own.
snakesInYard.mythsLead: These methods are often recommended, but they have no reliable effect. Spend time and money on yard management instead.
snakesInYard.appearTitle: What to do if a snake is in the yard
snakesInYard.appearBody: Do not try to catch or kill it — that is dangerous and often targets a harmless species. Watch from a distance, leave an exit open, and call the right service when you need help.
snakesInYard.contactBiteBody: Call 112 immediately. Stay calm, do not move the bitten arm or leg, and avoid home remedies (cutting, sucking, tourniquets).
snakesInYard.contactAgencyBody: Call them — they can help catch the reptile safely. Do not attempt it yourself.
snakesInYard.faqIntro: Short answers — practice is above; species detail lives in the atlas.
snakesInYard.faq1Q: Is there a product that repels snakes 100%?
snakesInYard.faq1A: No. The most effective approach is reducing shelter and food. Repellent sprays, sulfur, and similar methods do not deliver reliable results. Even after yard management, one may still appear — but it will not stay.
snakesInYard.faq2Q: Why do snakes come into the yard?
snakesInYard.faq2A: Mainly for shelter and food. Tall grass, logs, stones, building materials, and rodents make a yard more attractive.
snakesInYard.faq3Q: Do milk, sulfur, or sprays work?
snakesInYard.faq3A: No — these are common myths. Yard management works better: cut grass, remove shelter, and control rodents.
snakesInYard.faq4Q: What if a snake is already in the yard?
snakesInYard.faq4A: Do not touch it or try to catch it. Watch from a distance and leave an exit. If you need the snake removed safely, call the Animal Monitoring Agency: 032 272 16 00.
snakesInYard.faq5Q: What if a snake bites someone?
snakesInYard.faq5A: Call 112 immediately. Stay calm, do not move the bitten arm or leg, and do not use home remedies (cutting, sucking, tourniquets). This page is educational and does not replace medical advice.
snakesInYard.faq6A: No. In Georgia, non-venomous species are more common and are often confused with vipers. Compare profiles in the atlas before acting out of fear.
snakesInYard.ctaTitle: Identify the species — don’t act on fear alone
snakesInYard.ctaBody: Yard management lowers risk. If you see a snake, the atlas helps with identification and a safer decision.

snakeQuiz.practiceTitle: How to read a snake in a still frame
snakeQuiz.practiceLead: This page is a quiz, not a field-safety lesson. The question “venomous or harmless?” is answered on the identify guide. Here you get one frame from Georgia, four names, and time to train your eye on the atlas catalog.
snakeQuiz.practiceP1: Start with the head. A triangular silhouette from above often recalls a viper; an oval head in profile often belongs to a harmless colubrid. Is the neck clearly narrower than the head, or is it one mass? Many harmless snakes flatten the head and “borrow” that cue in a photo. One frame is not a verdict, but it is a start: if head and neck are separate, look toward colubrids first; if the head is broad and the neck short, compare viper profiles.
snakeQuiz.practiceP2: The pupil, if you can see it. A vertical slit in Georgia often points to a viper; a round pupil often points to a harmless snake. Light changes the cue, and many field photos hide it entirely. If the eye is a blur, do not guess from the pupil alone. Scale sheen is the same trap: a wet grass snake and a dry viper can both look glossy in one crop.
snakeQuiz.practiceP3: Then the pattern. Zigzag, spots, stripes, a plain back — that is what the quiz asks you to see in a second. The Caucasian viper and the grass snake sit close in photographs: both can show a dark back on a pale ground. The split is often head shape, keeled scales, and whether a yellow collar is visible. The smooth snake and the Transcaucasian viper are the same trap at another angle — small, brown, against forest litter.
snakeQuiz.practiceP4: Habitat in the background (stream, rock, steppe, leaf litter) helps, but the quiz does not ask where you are standing. Field safety lives on another page: marks, risk, and what not to do. The job here is speed of the eye — so that before you open a species profile you already know what in the frame caught you. Below are six pairs this atlas confuses most often in photographs.
snakeQuiz.lookalikesTitle: Pairs that confuse a still photo
snakeQuiz.lookalikesLead: This is not field diagnosis. It is what the eye mixes in one frame — and where the quiz draws its distractor names.
snakeQuiz.lookalike1Body: The grass snake often shows a yellow collar and a round pupil; the Caucasian viper a broader head and a vertical pupil when visible. Both are photographed in western forest.
snakeQuiz.lookalike2Body: The dice snake is usually narrower-headed, with strongly keeled scales; the same viper is often shorter, with a sharper zigzag. A stream in the background can belong to either.
snakeQuiz.lookalike3Body: The smooth snake is small, smooth-scaled, round-headed. The Transcaucasian viper sits in the same browns, but the head is broader and the dorsal pattern breaks differently.
snakeQuiz.lookalike4Body: Dinnik’s viper is a high-mountain animal and still matches the smooth snake in size on a photo. Look for head width and the rhythm of the zigzag, not colour alone.
snakeQuiz.lookalike5Body: The Montpellier snake is long and fast, with a large eye; giurza is heavy, with a blunt snout. Size and head profile still split this pair in a photo, unless the crop is tight.
snakeQuiz.lookalike6Body: The glass lizard is a lizard: eyelids and an ear opening. The grass snake has neither. It never appears as a quiz option — it is here so a “snake” in a photo is not always a snake.
snakeQuiz.practiceGuideTitle: Field identification is not this page
snakeQuiz.practiceGuideBody: If you need venomous-versus-harmless logic in the field, that guide stands alone. This quiz only trains you on catalog photos.

lizardQuiz.practiceTitle: How to read a lizard in a still frame
lizardQuiz.practiceLead: This page is a quiz, not a field-identification lesson. The question “what lizard is this?” is answered on the identify guide. Here you get one frame, four names, and time to train your eye on the atlas catalog. The glass lizard is in this quiz because it is a lizard.
lizardQuiz.practiceP1: Start with the silhouette. A long legless body may be the glass lizard or the slow worm — both are lizards. The Caucasian agama is an agamid: a heavier head, often on rock. Darevskia are small rock lizards that look alike in colour.
lizardQuiz.practiceP2: Eyelids and an ear opening, if visible, point to a lizard and rule out a snake. The glass lizard has them; the grass snake does not. Snakes are not quiz options, but the landing pair is here so a “snake” in a photo is not always a snake.
lizardQuiz.practiceP3: Then pattern and size — only marks already on the profiles. Darevskia stay separate species here: colour is not ID. If the frame shows only a green or brown back, do not guess from colour alone.
lizardQuiz.practiceP4: Habitat in the background helps, but the quiz does not ask where you are. Field identification lives on another page. The job here is speed of the eye on catalog photos. Below are four pairs from this atlas’s lizard identify guide.
lizardQuiz.lookalikesTitle: Pairs that confuse a still photo
lizardQuiz.lookalikesLead: This is not field diagnosis. It is what the eye mixes in one frame — the same pairs as on the lizard identify guide.
lizardQuiz.lookalike1Body: The Caucasian agama is an agamid; the Caspian gecko is smaller, with different skin texture. Both are photographed on rock.
lizardQuiz.lookalike2Body: The agama is not a Darevskia. Portschinsky’s rock lizard is smaller; colour does not split this pair.
lizardQuiz.lookalike3Body: The glass lizard is a large legless lizard; the slow worm is smaller and smoother. Both have eyelids. The slow worm is a checklist candidate.
lizardQuiz.lookalike4Body: The glass lizard is a lizard: eyelids and an ear opening. The grass snake is a snake. The grass snake is not a quiz option.
lizardQuiz.lookalike5Body: Darevskia species sit close in colour. The quiz keeps them separate — colour is not identification.
lizardQuiz.lookalike6Body: The glass lizard is in this quiz pool because it is a lizard. It is never an option in the snake quiz.
lizardQuiz.practiceGuideTitle: Field identification is not this page
lizardQuiz.practiceGuideBody: If you need field logic — photo, size, colour, range — the guide “What lizard is this?” stands alone. For Darevskia, colour is not enough.
lizardQuiz.faq1A: You see a photo and pick one of four species. After you answer, you get instant feedback, a short explanation, and a link to the species page.
lizardQuiz.faq2A: No. The quiz works without registration and does not ask for personal data.
lizardQuiz.faq3A: The default round is 10 questions. Each has one correct species and three plausible lookalikes.
lizardQuiz.faq4Q: Where do the photos and names come from?
lizardQuiz.faq4A: The quiz uses the published reptiles.ge lizard catalog and field photos — there is no second species database. Darevskia species stay separate.

spiderVenomous.metaDescription: The medically significant spider in this atlas is the karakurt. Argiope is not a black widow. What to look for, what not to handle, and when to call 112 after a bite.
spiderVenomous.keywords: venomous spiders Georgia, karakurt, black widow, false karakurt, Argiope
spiderVenomous.heroImageAlt: Karakurt — black female with a globular abdomen
spiderVenomous.title: Venomous spiders in Georgia?
spiderVenomous.subtitle: In this atlas the medically significant spider is the karakurt. Argiope is not a black widow. Do not pick a spider up; if bitten, call 112.
spiderVenomous.summaryTitle: What to know in the first minute
spiderVenomous.summaryLead: The Georgia atlas has four spider profiles. Only the karakurt (Latrodectus tredecimguttatus) is High risk. The other three are Harmless in the atlas — that does not mean a bite never hurts.
spiderVenomous.summary1: Do not pick up or press a spider — bites usually happen on contact.
spiderVenomous.summary2: A yellow-and-black orb web with a white zigzag is Argiope, not a karakurt.
spiderVenomous.summary3: A brown spider with a band at the front of the abdomen is often the false karakurt.
spiderVenomous.summary4: If bitten, call 112 — do not wait for symptoms and do not cut the bite.
spiderVenomous.guideTitle: Why this is not a US article
spiderVenomous.guideP1: A Georgian search for black widow often means Latrodectus mactans. The World Spider Catalog treats that species as native to North America. What is confirmed here is the Mediterranean / European karakurt — L. tredecimguttatus. Older records often listed Caucasian material as a subspecies of L. mactans.
spiderVenomous.guideP2: The atlas has four profiles, not Georgia's 659-spider list (Otto 2022). Named karakurt records are Tbilisi, Gori, Aspindza, and the Shiraki and Eldari plains. Other regions are not coloured unless a profile names a record. Do not treat the spider photos on this page as Georgia-field shots.
spiderVenomous.idTitle: How do we tell which spider it is?
spiderVenomous.idBody: Colour is not enough. Web type, abdomen shape, and size work together. If unsure, do not pick it up — open the profile.
spiderVenomous.id1Body: Karakurt and false karakurt spin an irregular cobweb — often near the ground, among stones and debris. Argiope spins a large orb web, often with a white zigzag (stabilimentum).
spiderVenomous.id2Body: The female is about 7–15 mm, glossy black, with a globular abdomen. The back often has red spots; some adults are entirely black — Seropian et al. 2024 note that the thirteen spots often fade in mature females. An American hourglass is not a required mark.
spiderVenomous.id3Body: Steatoda paykulliana is usually brown, with a red or yellow band on the front edge of the abdomen. Harmless in the atlas, but a bite can hurt. This is not a karakurt.
spiderVenomous.id4Body: Argiope bruennichi is yellow-and-black and sits at the web centre. A. lobata is paler, with a lobed abdomen. Both are orb-weavers and Harmless in the atlas.
spiderVenomous.dontLead: A spider is not a pest to crush. Handling it raises the chance of a bite.
spiderVenomous.dont1: Do not pick it up or press it — not even to check.
spiderVenomous.dont2: Do not destroy every garden web: Argiope catches insects and is not a black widow.
spiderVenomous.dont3: Do not cut, suck, or burn a bite. Call 112.
spiderVenomous.speciesBody: {count} profiles — for comparison, not a full arachnofauna. If the marks match a karakurt, open that page.
spiderVenomous.mythsLead: Georgian internet copy often describes spiders with American names.
spiderVenomous.myth1False: Myth: a yellow-and-black garden spider is a black widow.
spiderVenomous.myth1True: Reality: that is almost always Argiope — orb web, larger, Harmless in the atlas.
spiderVenomous.myth2False: Myth: the American black widow (L. mactans) lives in Georgia.
spiderVenomous.myth2True: Reality: L. tredecimguttatus is what is confirmed here. L. mactans is a different species.
spiderVenomous.myth3False: Myth: a small spider cannot be dangerous.
spiderVenomous.myth3True: Reality: a karakurt female is 7–15 mm. Size does not rule out risk.
spiderVenomous.myth4False: Myth: every black spider is a karakurt.
spiderVenomous.myth4True: Reality: the false karakurt is also dark. The front band and the web separate them; if unsure, do not pick it up.
spiderVenomous.faqIntro: Short answers. Bite steps are on a separate guide.
spiderVenomous.faq1Q: Is there a venomous spider in Georgia?
spiderVenomous.faq1A: The High-risk species in the atlas is the karakurt. Argiope is Harmless. A false-karakurt bite can hurt, but that is not a karakurt.
spiderVenomous.faq2A: No. Argiope is an orb-weaver with a yellow-and-black or lobed abdomen. The karakurt is small, with an irregular web close to the ground.
spiderVenomous.faq3A: Harmless in the atlas. A bite can hurt. Do not pick it up. For severe symptoms, call 112.
spiderVenomous.faq4Q: Is the karakurt everywhere in Georgia?
spiderVenomous.faq4A: No. The map colours only named records: Tbilisi, Gori, Aspindza, Shiraki, Eldari. Massive in the Caucasus does not mean every region.
spiderVenomous.faq5Q: What should I do if a spider bites me?
spiderVenomous.faq5A: Call 112. Do not cut, suck, or catch the spider. Steps are on the spider-bite guide.
spiderVenomous.faq6Q: Can I pick a spider up?
spiderVenomous.faq6A: No. Handling it is what raises the chance of a bite.
spiderVenomous.ctaTitle: From a mark to a profile
spiderVenomous.ctaBody: Open a species or the bite guide. First rule: do not pick it up; after a bite, 112.

spiderBite.metaTitle: Spider bite — what should you do?
spiderBite.metaDescription: Spider bite in Georgia: call 112. Do not cut, suck, or catch the spider. A karakurt bite is medically significant. Educational page — not a medical protocol.
spiderBite.keywords: spider bite Georgia, spider bit me, karakurt bite, 112
spiderBite.heroImageAlt: Karakurt — black female with a globular abdomen
spiderBite.title: Spider bite in Georgia — what should you do?
spiderBite.subtitle: If a spider has bitten you, the first step is 112. This page is educational and does not replace a clinician or emergency care.
spiderBite.disclaimerTitle: Bitten by a spider? Call 112 immediately
spiderBite.disclaimerBody: If a spider has bitten you in Georgia, call 112 and seek emergency medical care. Stay calm. Wash the bite with soap and water. Do not cut, suck, or catch the spider.
spiderBite.summary2: Wash with soap and water; a cold cloth or ice may ease pain.
spiderBite.summary3: Do not cut, suck, or try to remove venom.
spiderBite.summary4: Do not catch the spider. Identify it only if safe — from a distance or a photo.
spiderBite.disclaimerNote: Only medical staff decide treatment. The steps here are educational first-response points from 112 and CDC/NIOSH public guidance — not a medical protocol.
spiderBite.doTitle: What to do after a spider bite
spiderBite.do1Body: Immediately. 112 is Georgia's single emergency number. Do not wait for symptoms.
spiderBite.do2Body: CDC/NIOSH: remain calm. Extra movement is not needed while you wait for help.
spiderBite.do3Body: Wash the bite. That is cleanliness, not venom removal.
spiderBite.do4Body: CDC/NIOSH names a cold cloth or ice to reduce pain. This is not treatment.
spiderBite.do5Body: Home methods do not replace care. A photo of the spider can wait if it is safe — 112 comes first.
spiderBite.dont1Body: Cutting the wound does not remove venom and causes harm.
spiderBite.dont2Body: Sucking venom by mouth or device does not work. CDC/NIOSH rules out trying to remove venom.
spiderBite.dont3Body: Catching it often causes another bite. Identify only if safe.
spiderBite.dont4Title: Do not burn the bite or use folk remedies
spiderBite.dont4Body: Burning, alcohol, or unproven methods are not treatment and waste time.
spiderBite.dont5Title: Do not delay 112 to identify the species
spiderBite.dont5Body: Call and seek care first. The profile can wait.
spiderBite.symptomsIntro: Symptoms depend on the species. Below are possible signs, mainly karakurt latrodectism (Nentwig et al.) — not a diagnostic list.
spiderBite.symptomsUrgent: Do not wait for symptoms before calling 112. Absence of symptoms does not mean the bite is safe.
spiderBite.symptom1: Pain at the bite — in latrodectism often severe and lasting
spiderBite.symptom2: Pain that worsens in the first hour; often radiates into a limb or the abdomen
spiderBite.symptom5: Fever or neuromuscular signs — in fewer cases
spiderBite.symptom6: Raised blood pressure — in fewer cases
spiderBite.symptomsNote: Nentwig et al.: pain is severe and lasting in about two thirds of cases; pain usually 1–2 days, other signs 1–4 days. Death is rare in modern European material — that does not make the bite mild. The list is not complete.
spiderBite.dangerTitle: When is a spider bite especially concerning?
spiderBite.dangerIntro: Every suspected bite is a 112 case. The High-risk species on this page is the karakurt.
spiderBite.danger1: Severe lasting pain, sweating, nausea, or other general signs.
spiderBite.danger2: Children often experience heavier effects because of smaller body mass.
spiderBite.danger3: If the spider looks like a karakurt, or the bite happened among stones and debris.
spiderBite.danger4: If you did not see the spider but suspect a bite — still call 112.
spiderBite.contextTitle: Is every spider bite the same?
spiderBite.contextBody: No. The medically significant species in the atlas is the karakurt. Argiope is Harmless. The false karakurt is Harmless in the atlas; steatodism is milder — that is Australian Steatoda material (Isbister and Gray 2003), not a Georgian series. Species comparison belongs in the <venomous>venomous-spider guide</venomous>, not at the bite scene.
spiderBite.contextNote: The brown recluse (Loxosceles reclusa) is not in this atlas for Georgia. Do not import American names onto a bite here.
spiderBite.unseenEyebrow: If you did not see the spider
spiderBite.unseenTitle: What if I did not see the spider?
spiderBite.unseenBody: Still call 112. Do not delay the call for identification. A distant photo can help later if it is safe. Do not catch the spider.
spiderBite.unseenId: Species comparison later — in the <venomous>venomous-spider guide</venomous>, only after 112 is underway.
spiderBite.speciesTitle: Which spider on this page is High risk?
spiderBite.speciesBody: Below is the atlas's {count} High-risk spider — the karakurt. Full context: <index>spiders hub</index>. After a bite, 112 first.
spiderBite.sourcesTitle: What this page is based on
spiderBite.sourcesIntro: Medical advice cites external authoritative sources. Species come from the atlas. This page is not a medical institution.
spiderBite.sourceExt1Body: Georgia's single emergency number. After a bite, this is the first action.
spiderBite.sourceExt2Body: Stay calm; wash with soap and water; cold cloth or ice; do not try to remove venom; seek professional care; identify the spider only if safe.
spiderBite.sourceExt3Title: Isbister and White 2004 — Clinical consequences of spider bites
spiderBite.sourceExt3Body: Clinical review of spider bites. DOI: 10.1016/j.toxicon.2004.02.006.
spiderBite.sourceExt4Title: Nentwig et al. 2013 — Verified spider bites in Switzerland
spiderBite.sourceExt4Body: Verified bites; latrodectism severity is read with the species-level account. DOI: 10.1016/j.toxicon.2013.07.020.
spiderBite.sourceSite1Body: Risk level and identification from atlas data — not a medical protocol.
spiderBite.sourceSite2Body: Page structure is prepared by Reptiles.ge from the sources above.

spiderBite.editorialDisclaimer: The page is educational and does not replace a clinician or 112.
spiderBite.faqIntro: Short answers. Detail is above; medical decisions belong with 112 and clinicians.
spiderBite.faq1Q: What should I do first after a spider bite?
spiderBite.faq1A: Call 112. Stay calm, wash with soap and water. Do not cut, suck, or catch the spider.
spiderBite.faq2Q: Can I cut a bite or suck out venom?
spiderBite.faq2A: No. CDC/NIOSH rules out removing venom. Cutting and sucking cause harm.
spiderBite.faq3Q: Should I catch the spider so doctors know the species?
spiderBite.faq3A: No. Catching it often causes another bite. A distant photo is enough if safe.
spiderBite.faq4Q: Is every spider bite medically serious?
spiderBite.faq4A: No. The High-risk species on this page is the karakurt. Argiope is Harmless. A false-karakurt bite can hurt. Do not judge risk yourself — call 112.
spiderBite.faq5A: The syndrome after a karakurt bite. Nentwig: pain is severe and lasting in about two thirds of cases; sweating is common; nausea and other signs less so. Death is rare in modern European material, but the bite is not mild.
spiderBite.faq6Q: Is a false-karakurt bite the same?
spiderBite.faq6A: No. Harmless in the atlas. Steatodism is milder — Isbister and Gray 2003 is Australian Steatoda material, not a Georgian series.
spiderBite.faq7Q: Does the brown recluse live in Georgia?
spiderBite.faq7A: Loxosceles reclusa is not in this atlas. Do not import American names onto a Georgian bite.
spiderBite.faq8Q: What if I did not see the spider?
spiderBite.faq8A: Still call 112. Do not delay the call for identification.
spiderBite.ctaBody: Species comparison is on the venomous-spider guide. After a bite, 112 still comes first.

mammalJackalYard.metaTitle: A jackal in the yard — what should you do?
mammalJackalYard.metaDescription: A jackal in a Georgian yard: do not feed it. Secure food and poultry. After a bite, call 112. How to tell it from a fox or a wolf.
mammalJackalYard.keywords: jackal in the yard, golden jackal Georgia, Canis aureus, jackal poultry
mammalJackalYard.heroImageAlt: Golden jackal — yellowish-grey coat, short tail with a dark tip
mammalJackalYard.title: A jackal in the yard — what should you do?
mammalJackalYard.subtitle: Do not feed it. Food and unsecured poultry attract it. After a bite, call 112 — this page is educational.
mammalJackalYard.summaryTitle: What to know in the first minute
mammalJackalYard.summaryLead: The golden jackal (Canis aureus) is a native resident in Georgia. It follows food into a yard — not because it hunts people.
mammalJackalYard.summary1: Do not feed it and do not pick it up.
mammalJackalYard.summary2: Secure poultry and food waste — an unsecured yard can lose birds.
mammalJackalYard.summary3: From a fox it differs by a shorter tail with a dark tip, not a white one.
mammalJackalYard.summary4: After a bite, call 112. Rabies is named among wild carnivores.
mammalJackalYard.whyTitle: Why does a jackal enter a yard?
mammalJackalYard.whyLead: The jackal is an opportunistic omnivore. A yard is attractive when food is easy.
mammalJackalYard.why1Body: Carrion, slaughter waste, open refuse, and unsecured poultry sit in the species' broad menu. Local shares are not measured here.
mammalJackalYard.why2Body: The species is more frequent in lowlands and farmland. Shakarashvili et al. 2020 treat it as common in Georgia and note higher elevations than before, where it was once rare.
mammalJackalYard.actionsTitle: What should I do if a jackal is in the yard?
mammalJackalYard.actionsLead: The aim is not to kill or poison it — remove food and keep distance.
mammalJackalYard.action1Body: Hand-feeding or leftover food brings it back. Keep dogs away.
mammalJackalYard.action2Body: An unsecured yard can lose poultry or small livestock. That is opportunistic feeding, not hunting people.
mammalJackalYard.action3Body: Do not pick it up, especially if it approaches without fear or is aggressive. A daytime sighting can also be normal.
mammalJackalYard.action4Body: Poison reaches other animals, and there is no how-to here. Conflict starts by removing food.
mammalJackalYard.identifyLead: Three canids are in the atlas. Colour is not enough — tail, size, and silhouette work together.
mammalJackalYard.identify1: Jackal: head-body often 70–85 cm; tail shorter than a fox's, tip usually dark, not white.
mammalJackalYard.identify2: Fox: finer muzzle, longer tail, often a white tip, black behind the ears.
mammalJackalYard.identify3: Wolf: much larger, longer-legged, heavier head. A free-ranging dog can match the size.
mammalJackalYard.mythsLead: Jackals are often mixed up with foxes or a strange dog.
mammalJackalYard.myth1False: Myth: the jackal was introduced to Georgia.
mammalJackalYard.myth1True: Reality: IUCN lists it as native here. It is on national mammal lists.
mammalJackalYard.myth2False: Myth: a white tail tip marks a jackal.
mammalJackalYard.myth2True: Reality: a white tail tip is more a fox mark. The jackal's tail is shorter, with a dark tip.
mammalJackalYard.myth3True: Reality: in a yard they follow food and unsecured poultry. They have no venom; the risk is a bite and rabies.
mammalJackalYard.myth4False: Myth: jackals occur only on the eastern lowland.
mammalJackalYard.myth4True: Reality: they are more frequent in the lowland, but Shakarashvili 2020 also notes higher elevations. At Fonichala in 2020–21 the jackal was the most frequent mammal on camera (Kalandarishvili 2024). A named photo is from Lagodekhi, 2025.
mammalJackalYard.contactBody: A bite is an emergency. Yard conflict starts by removing food — this page does not invent an agency number.
mammalJackalYard.contactBiteTitle: If a jackal has bitten you
mammalJackalYard.contactBiteBody: Call 112. A bite or saliva can carry rabies risk. Wash the wound; the next step belongs to a clinician.
mammalJackalYard.contactHelpBody: Secure poultry and close waste. Do not feed. The profile is for identification — not a poisoning guide.
mammalJackalYard.faqTitle: A jackal in the yard — frequently asked questions
mammalJackalYard.faqIntro: Short answers. Depth lives on the profile.
mammalJackalYard.faq1Q: What should I do if a jackal is in the yard?
mammalJackalYard.faq1A: Do not feed it or pick it up. Watch from a distance. Secure poultry and refuse. After a bite, 112.
mammalJackalYard.faq2Q: How do I tell a jackal from a fox?
mammalJackalYard.faq2A: The jackal's tail is shorter, with a dark tip. A fox has a longer tail, often with a white tip. Head-body is often 70–85 cm.
mammalJackalYard.faq3A: They are not venomous. They can bite. In a yard they follow food, not people as prey. Rabies is named among wild carnivores.
mammalJackalYard.faq4A: No. Feeding brings it back and raises risk.
mammalJackalYard.faq5A: It can, in an unsecured yard. That is opportunistic feeding. Secure the birds — do not poison.
mammalJackalYard.faq6Q: What should I do after a bite?
mammalJackalYard.faq6A: Call 112. Wash the wound. Rabies risk is a medical decision, not a diagnosis on this page.
mammalJackalYard.ctaTitle: From the yard to a profile
mammalJackalYard.ctaBody: Open the jackal, fox, or wolf page. In the yard the first rule is: do not feed; after a bite, 112.

mammalBear.disclaimerBody: Do not approach, do not feed, do not let a dog go. Cubs mean the mother is nearby. If it has injured you — call 112.
mammalBear.summary1: Georgia has only the brown bear (Ursus arctos).
mammalBear.summary2: Do not approach and do not feed. Make noise on the trail so you do not surprise it.
mammalBear.summary3: A cub means the mother is nearby. Do not let a dog go.
mammalBear.summary4: If injured, call 112. Do not kill it — EN on the 2014 Red List.
mammalBear.disclaimerNote: These are educational first steps from the profile and named sources — not a field combat protocol and not a North American play-dead or fight rule.
mammalBear.doTitle: What to do if you meet a bear
mammalBear.do1Body: Back away slowly. Do not approach for a photo or to drive it off.
mammalBear.do2Body: Sound lowers the chance of a surprise meeting — especially a mother with cubs or an animal on a carcass.
mammalBear.do3Body: Do not let it go. A dog can bring a bear back to people.
mammalBear.do4Body: Camp food should be closed. Feeding brings the animal back and raises conflict.
mammalBear.do5Body: 112 is Georgia's single emergency number. Do not wait until it sorts itself out.
mammalBear.dont1Body: It is a large animal: it can bite or strike if you meet it by surprise.
mammalBear.dont2Body: Feeding trains conflict. Beehive and livestock loss is real in some villages — especially around Borjomi-Kharagauli — that does not mean the bear hunts people.
mammalBear.dont3Title: Do not let a dog go
mammalBear.dont3Body: A chase brings the bear back. Hold the dog or withdraw with it.
mammalBear.dont4Title: Do not import North American rules
mammalBear.dont4Body: Play dead or fight a grizzly is not a protocol here. Georgia has no other bear species.
mammalBear.dont5Body: Hunting is not allowed. Decree No. 190 of 2014 lists the species as EN.
mammalBear.dangerTitle: When is a meeting especially concerning?
mammalBear.dangerIntro: Every close meeting asks for space. Below are situations with higher risk.
mammalBear.danger1: A mother with cubs — a cub can look like a dog from a distance; the mother is nearby.
mammalBear.danger2: A surprise meeting at a carcass or a den.
mammalBear.danger3: A dog chase that brings the bear back to people.
mammalBear.danger4: Injury — then 112, not a home method.
mammalBear.contextBody: Only the brown bear. Polar and American black bears do not occur here. Lortkipanidze 2010 names three areas: the Greater Caucasus, the Lesser Caucasus, and the extreme east — including Vashlovani. Other mammals are on the <mammals>mammals hub</mammals>.

mammalBear.faqTitle: Meeting a bear — frequently asked questions
mammalBear.faqIntro: Short answers. Depth lives on the profile.
mammalBear.faq1Q: What should I do if I meet a bear?
mammalBear.faq1A: Give it space, do not approach, do not feed, do not let a dog go. If injured, 112.
mammalBear.faq2Q: Should I play dead or fight?
mammalBear.faq2A: Neither is a protocol on this page. Those are North American tips for another context. Here: back away, do not approach.
mammalBear.faq3Q: Is there another bear in Georgia?
mammalBear.faq3A: No. Only the brown bear. Polar and American black bears do not occur here.
mammalBear.faq4Q: Why is it seen near a village?
mammalBear.faq4A: Loss of hives and livestock is real in some villages, especially around Borjomi-Kharagauli. That is conflict, not hunting people.
mammalBear.faq5A: No. It is EN on the Red List (Decree No. 190, 2014). Hunting is not allowed.
mammalBear.faq6Q: What if it has injured me?
mammalBear.faq6A: Call 112. This page is educational and does not replace a clinician.
mammalBear.ctaBody: The profile is for status and range. In a meeting the first rule is space; if injured, 112.

lizardHouse.metaTitle: A lizard in the house — what should you do?
lizardHouse.metaDescription: A lizard in a Georgian house is often the Caspian gecko: Harmless, do not kill it. The Caucasian agama is not a gecko. Removal: 032 272 16 00.
lizardHouse.keywords: lizard in the house, Caspian gecko, gecko Tbilisi, Caucasian agama, Tenuidactylus caspius
lizardHouse.heroImageAlt: Caspian gecko on a wall — vertical pupil, expanded toes
lizardHouse.title: A lizard in the house — what should you do?
lizardHouse.subtitle: Often a Caspian gecko on the wall. Harmless. Do not kill it. This page is house practice — not the What lizard is this? identification guide.
lizardHouse.summaryTitle: What to know in the first minute
lizardHouse.summaryLead: In Tarkhnishvili et al. 2026 the only gecko on the checklist is the Caspian gecko (Tenuidactylus caspius). Harmless in the atlas.
lizardHouse.summary1: Do not kill it or press it to check.
lizardHouse.summary2: A vertical pupil and expanded toes point to a gecko, not a Caucasian agama.
lizardHouse.summary3: The natural range is the extreme south-east; urban exclaves include the Black Sea coast.
lizardHouse.summary4: If you need it removed — Animal Monitoring Agency: 032 272 16 00.
lizardHouse.whyTitle: Why is a lizard in the house?
lizardHouse.whyLead: A gecko climbs vertical surfaces and hides in cracks. A house is often warmth and insects, not an attack.
lizardHouse.why1Body: By day it hides in cracks; after dusk it shows on walls. A vertical pupil belongs with night and twilight activity.
lizardHouse.why2Body: The natural range is the extreme south-east. Urban populations are named, including the Black Sea coast. Barcodes are from Tbilisi and the Samukhi plain; the figure is Dedoplistskaro.
lizardHouse.actionsTitle: What should I do if a lizard is in the house?
lizardHouse.actionsLead: The aim is not to kill it — humane exclusion and closing cracks.
lizardHouse.action1Body: Lizards in this atlas are not venomous to people. The Caspian gecko is Harmless.
lizardHouse.action2Body: Open a window or door toward the room where it is on the wall. Do not grab it — skin and tail are fragile.
lizardHouse.action3Body: It stays where it enters. Close gaps on walls and frames — that is exclusion, not poisoning.
lizardHouse.action4Body: If you cannot move it yourself — Animal Monitoring Agency: 032 272 16 00. Do not force a catch.
lizardHouse.identifyLead: On a house wall it is often a gecko. The Caucasian agama is a diurnal rock agamid. Full comparison is on the identify guide.
lizardHouse.identify1: Caspian gecko: vertical pupil, expanded toes, night or twilight activity on a wall.
lizardHouse.identify2: Caucasian agama (Paralaudakia caucasia): a diurnal agamid with a triangular head, on rock — not a gecko.
lizardHouse.identify3: This page does not replace the lizard identification guide (What lizard is this?).
lizardHouse.mythsLead: A house lizard is often called venomous or taken for a Caucasian agama.
lizardHouse.myth1False: Myth: the house gecko is venomous.
lizardHouse.myth1True: Reality: Harmless in the atlas. Venom risk here concerns some snakes, not lizards.
lizardHouse.myth2False: Myth: a lizard on the wall is a Caucasian agama.
lizardHouse.myth2True: Reality: the agama is a diurnal rock agamid. On a wall at night it is often the Caspian gecko.
lizardHouse.myth3False: Myth: the gecko is evenly spread across Georgia.
lizardHouse.myth3True: Reality: the natural range is the extreme south-east; cities have exclaves. The map is not invented.
lizardHouse.myth4False: Myth: I must kill it to get it out of the house.
lizardHouse.myth4True: Reality: humane exclusion and closing cracks is enough. If needed, 032 272 16 00.
lizardHouse.contactTitle: When you cannot move it yourself
lizardHouse.contactBody: This page does not open 112 — the gecko is Harmless. For removal, the same agency as on the snakes-in-the-yard guide is named.
lizardHouse.contactAgencyBody: Call if you need the lizard removed safely. Do not force a catch yourself.
lizardHouse.faqTitle: A lizard in the house — frequently asked questions
lizardHouse.faqIntro: Short answers. Species depth is on the profile; field comparison is on the identify guide.
lizardHouse.faq1Q: What lizard is on the house wall?
lizardHouse.faq1A: Often the Caspian gecko — the only gecko on the checklist. Vertical pupil and expanded toes. The Caucasian agama is another family.
lizardHouse.faq3A: No. Give it an exit and close the cracks.
lizardHouse.faq4Q: How does it differ from the Caucasian agama?
lizardHouse.faq4A: The agama is a diurnal agamid with a triangular head, on rock. The gecko is on a wall at night, with a vertical pupil.
lizardHouse.faq5Q: Who do I call to remove it?
lizardHouse.faq5A: Animal Monitoring Agency: 032 272 16 00. 112 is not opened on this page — the species is Harmless.
lizardHouse.faq6Q: Is this the same as the lizard identification guide?
lizardHouse.faq6A: No. This is house practice. What lizard is this? is a separate page for Darevskia and other species.
lizardHouse.ctaTitle: From the house to a profile
lizardHouse.ctaBody: Open the Caspian gecko or the identify guide. In the house the first rule is: do not kill it.
